title: 29. The Charity of the Head
purpose: It compiles the Ismaili legal rulings on zakat al-Fitr — its measure, its timing, who owes it and on whose behalf — together with a few residual rulings on zakat generally.

points.text: Answering a question about the Indian custom of mixing four grains (rice, maize, wheat, salt) and taking their monetary value, the reply is that reliance is on the Book of the Pillars: a sa of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins.
entities: Book of the Pillars of Islam

points.text: A reported saying holds that the fitra should be from the best of what one eats and the purest of what one stores, yet mixing it from everything eaten during Ramadan suffices, and one who ate nothing but barley may give barley.

Against the objection that obligatory duties may not be performed outside their appointed times, the answer given is that delivering the fitra to a rightful recipient suffices whenever done, since no fixed time was set for advancing or delaying it — the sole prohibition being that one must not break the fast before delivering it.
Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that a dhimmi who accepts Islam before dawn on the day of Fitr owes zakat al-Fitr, while one who converts after dawn owes nothing.

Reports state the fitra is paid on behalf of the mukatab; the Landmarks of Religion that it is due for a child born before dawn on the day of Fitr; and the Book of the Pillars that it has also been said to be paid for the child still in the womb.

The Landmarks of Religion gives the sa as four and a half Meccan ratls, five ratls less a third by the ratl of Medina, and nine and a tenth Baghdadi ratls, while the Selected Book allows a sa of dried curd or half a sa of wheat.

The thirteenth Mustansiriyya session, following on the prior session about zakat owed by the wealthy, presents zakat al-Fitr as the zakat obligatory in every condition and even upon those of small means, comprising seven obligations and twelve Sunnah practices.
The seven obligations are that a man pay it for himself, for the elder and the younger of his household, the free and the enslaved among them, and the males and the females among them.

The Sunnah practices include bringing it from the middle sort of what one eats (a sa of wheat, barley, dates, or raisins — half a sa sufficing only for wheat, the sa being four mudds), handing it to the Imam or his appointee, bringing it out before the breaking of the fast, making it up if delayed, and giving its value in silver or gold if one lacks the food; a woman with no husband present pays for herself and her dependants.
The Inner Nursing cites the Prophet's saying that the fitra is lawful neither for him nor for the people of his house.

Zayd ibn Muhammad in the Concealed Epistle holds that the Prophet obliged every Muslim head — male, female, small, great, even an infant born that day, and the child in the womb — to pay a sa, and explains that zakat al-Fitr is therefore named 'the charity of the head'.

Al-Qadi al-Numan's Mafatih al-Nima distinguishes fitra from ordinary charity by timing — before sunrise it is fitra, after sunrise mere sadaqa — and defines fitra as bringing out what is owed to God and to His appointed guardian, as ransom and offering.

Two residual riddle-rulings hold that zakat is lawful to a man who owns a thousand dinars but owes a thousand (so no zakat is due from him), and to a well-off polytheist who has found no Muslim to receive his zakat, who then has more right to it than anyone.
